title: Angelini on what central-bank cooperation can preserve when governments disagree
summary: Paolo Angelini argues that international central-bank cooperation retains economic value even when governments disagree on broader policy. Speaking at the opening of the Soft Power Conference on 29 January, the Bank of Italy’s Deputy Governor offers one concrete example: central banks and supervisors had maintained enough agreement to continue work on physical climate risks to financial stability. Some participants would have preferred a more ambitious outcome. In his judgement, keeping a narrower area of technical cooperation alive also preserves the ability to tackle other issues later. His remarks concern the institutions through which risks are assessed. They contain no policy-rate decision, regulatory timetable or recommendation for an asset position (pp. 1–2).

Angelini starts from Joseph Nye’s conception of power exercised through attraction and persuasion. He sees growing reliance on military force and economic pressure, together with increased protectionism, fragmentation of trade and cyber warfare. These developments strain the relationships on which cooperation has depended. He describes willingness to cooperate as exceptionally low by the standards of recent decades. The decline is his qualitative judgement. The short address supplies no historical series with which to estimate its magnitude, and it does not translate that judgement into a probability of any particular trade or financial regime.

The link to economic decisions runs through trust. A central bank’s credibility, predictability and ability to communicate can influence how households, businesses and financial investors form expectations. Those expectations in turn affect decisions in the economy. The Global Soft Power Index, scheduled for presentation at the conference, serves as a prompt for the argument. Angelini calls the index authors’ evidence on economic benefits tentative. The underlying results, country scores and methods are absent from his remarks. A reader therefore cannot infer a country’s financing cost or expected growth rate from a purported change in its index rank on the strength of this speech (p. 1).

His more direct evidence concerns the persistence of working relationships. He names the IMF, World Bank, Basel Committee, BIS and Financial Stability Board as settings in which dialogue and compromise continue. The Financial Stability Board also includes government representatives. Established forums permit technical conversations on financial stability, digital innovation and politically sensitive subjects despite a less supportive international environment. This observation establishes a channel for coordination. It does not show that all members have agreed on one risk assessment or that they will implement standards in the same way.

Physical climate risk illustrates the difference. Supervisors can discuss how damage to assets or operations may affect intermediaries without first resolving every dispute about the wider climate agenda. Angelini considers agreement on that work pragmatic under the circumstances. He also recognises the dissatisfaction of those who would have preferred broader cooperation. The potential value is intertemporal: continued contact today leaves an institutional route available for discussion when interests diverge again. The address gives no stress-test assumptions, changes to capital requirements or cost estimates for banks. For a portfolio manager, the implication is correspondingly limited but material. Common discussion of a risk supports the case for examining comparable supervisory work across countries. An inference about a binding cross-border standard requires separate evidence of adoption, enforcement and timing (p. 2).

questions.question: Where has the agreement on physical risk changed actual supervision?
questions.detail: Angelini establishes a common topic for discussion but gives no examples of binding measures. Compare contemporaneous supervisory priorities, published stress-test designs and requests for bank disclosures across the relevant jurisdictions. A bank investor needs to know whether lenders face similar evidence requirements or materially different costs in different markets before inferring any effect on relative profitability.

questions.question: How much economic information is contained in the soft-power measure?
questions.detail: The remarks describe the conference evidence as tentative and do not provide its specification. Consult the index authors’ methodological material and ask whether measures of reputation have predictive content after accounting for institutions and economic performance, both of which could themselves influence reputation. This would determine whether the index contributes to a country-risk assessment beyond the information investors already use.

questions.question: Which parts of international technical cooperation could persist through a further political rupture?
questions.detail: The speaker documents dialogue within long-standing institutions and a compromise on a contested subject, without establishing the limits of that arrangement. Consult communiqués, published work programmes and national implementation reports to distinguish continuing meetings from jointly delivered outcomes. This matters when assessing whether an apparent cross-border regulatory consensus will support consistent treatment of the same risk on bank balance sheets.
